abstract: Evolutionary engineering can optimize microbial consortia through iterative ecological perturbation and selection. It remains unclear whether selection improves community function simply by enriching communities with the strongest individual contributors or whether it can also enrich communities with synergistic interactions among species. Here, we address this question by optimizing the initial composition of multispecies wine yeast inoculants. Each generation we independently perturb the starting abundance of each of six yeast strains, toggling it between two of six possible doses (from 0 to 10 CFU/mL), and select for two functions of contrasting complexity. Unlike previous studies focused on serially passaged communities, our approach optimizes the initial inoculum composition for single-batch fermentation, a mode of operation common to many biotechnological processes. Selecting for a function that all individual strains can independently contribute to results in inoculants that are enriched with the strongest contributors. In contrast, selecting for a function that no strain can perform alone yields more complex communities whose performance emerges from synergistic interactions. These findings show that evolutionary engineering can exploit both individual contributions and interspecies interactions to optimize microbial communities. Our approach can be adapted to optimize other microbial inoculants of low-to-medium diversity.
